content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies parameter fine-tuning in federated learning. The method is called FedPEFT. The idea is to start with a pre-trained model and fine-tune a small subset of model parameters to fit the model to new tasks. An extensive set of experiments have been conducted and some insights are discussed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Fine-tuning models is a main application scenario of federated learning in practice.
- This paper introduces a few options of which subset of parameters to fine tune, by introducing the FedPEFT-Bias, FedPEFT-Adapter and FedPEFT-Prompt approaches derived from related work and comparing their performances.
- The results and insights from experiments give some guidance on practical implementation.

Weakness:
- The logical steps of FedPEFT in Algorithm 1 is the same as standard federated averaging (FedAvg). The only difference is that only a subset of parameters are trained, but this does not make any logical or mathematical difference, because we can consider only the trainable parameters as parameters in the FedAvg algorithm while considering the fixed parameters as part of the fixed model logic. The FedPEFT-Bias, FedPEFT-Adapter and FedPEFT-Prompt approaches are also straightforward combinations with existing techniques. Therefore, the technical novelty of this work is limited.
- Although the experiments are extensive, their discussions can be improved. It would be particularly interesting to analyze the new and non-obvious observations. For example, among the FedPEFT approaches in Table 3, why does FedPEFT-Prompt give the best performance in the first two rows while FedPEFT-Bias gives the best performance in the other rows? It would be nice if a more concrete conclusion can be drawn on which of the FedPEFT-* methods should be chosen in which settings. Some implementation details can be moved to the appendix to give more room for comprehensive discussions in the main paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is generally clear, but the organization and discussion of results could be improved.

Quality: The quality is OK.

Novelty: The technical novelty is limited, but the empirical novelty is good.

Reproducibility: The algorithm seems easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper provides an empirical study on some fine-tuning methods applied to federated learning. The consideration of fine-tuning is not often seen in the federated learning literature. The findings can be useful in guiding the implementation of practical federated learning systems.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper applies parameter-efficient federated learning (including adapter, BiTFiT, prompt tuning) to federated learning, especially the accuracy and communication cost. The performance of their method is tested on CIFAR100 and PCam, in order to demonstrate the advantage of new method on accuracy, privacy, scarcity, and so on.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The paper is very clearly written and the presentation is great, especially Figure 1 and 2. The experiments are sufficient and well-designed. The results are convincing enough to allow further application of FedPEFT.

Weakness: I have deep concerns of the novelty (thus significance) and the citation correctness. For the novelty concern, see next section. I don't think the authors pay enough attention to credit original authors of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. To be concrete, in the last paragraph above Section 4, adapter is firstly introduced by Rebuffi et al., 2017 (Learning multiple visual domains
with residual adapters) in computer vision and Houlsby et al., 2019 in NLP. (Parameter-efficient transfer learning for NLP), both ahead of the authors' reference; the prompt tuning is firstly proposed (though for NLP) by  Li & Liang, 2021 and Lester et al., 2021); also bias-tuning may include Zaken et al. 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The overall clarity and quality of this paper is high, and my concern is on the novelty. This work is an empirical paper with mature techniques from PEFT and federated learning. If we consider federated learning as a special case of distributed learning, then PEFT has been extensively studied on federated learning: see Hu et al. "LORA: LOW-RANK ADAPTATION OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS" and Yu et al. "Differentially Private Fine-tuning of Language Models", which stated "Finally, we expect that (1) also gives a more communication-efficient method of fine-tuning in distributed settings such as federated learning, due to the significantly smaller number of parameters
learned during fine-tuning.". Although these work didn't focus on the communication cost, the novelty of this work may still be limited, thus the overall impact of this work may be small given that the empirical results do not raise new insights from new benchmarks or datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper has limited impact on the field, mainly due to the lack of novelty since both PEFT and federated learning have been studied extensively, separately and jointly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper present a federated learning method, based on pretrained representation. Instead of training a model from scratch, this paper shows that utilizing pretrained representation can significantly reduce the communication cost, while maintaining decent model performance. Benefiting from the representation, it brings extra knowledge to the federated learning system, and then only a small part of networks needs to tune during the federated learning system, for example, only training the bias term in each network component. Specifically, this paper presents three variants of FedPEFT system, which shows more favorable results than training from scratch with fewer communication costs and better model performance. To show the effectiveness, this work conducts experiments on CIFAR-100 and PCam datasets with vision transformers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ By applying a pretrained model and fine-tuning small parts of networks, the experiments show that the communication costs can be reduced significantly and model performance is much better than the train-from-scratch baselines. Many studies in federated learning focus on training a network from scratch, however, pretrained representation on large-scale datasets is not enough considered. Although in centralized training, pretrained representation is still useful to reduce the computations and reach to higher performance. Therefore, exploring more on leveraging pretrained representations in federated learning is necessary.

+ This paper presents three model variants. In general, those models perform well, and FedPEFT-Bias performs slightly better.

+ This paper provides some studies on differential privacy, where it further supports the motivation of federated learning to keep local data private.

Weakness:
- In FedPEFT-Prompt, an input embedding is learned, which will change the input channel of the next layer. How do you take the pertrained parameters?

- In the experiment, PCam dataset is applied, which is not popular in federated learning research area. Why not follow previous federated learning benchmark [b]? It will be easier to compare the proposed method with others.

- In the experiment, this paper set the client numbers and updated clients by themselves. It will be much better to follow previous work, that researchers can easily compare the performance from this method to previous ones.

- ImageNet-21k provides representations like objects, however, PCam is a medical analysis datasets. Why does fine-tuning perform worse than the proposed method? Do you have any intuition or explanation for the results ?

- The experiments would be better to show the results of applying other optimizers, in addition to FedAvg, for example, FedAdam.

- Can you also provide ResNet results? Usually, ViT has a larger capacity compared with ResNet. Is the improved performance from the memorized representation in ViT?

- Citing recent relevant work is necessary [a].

[a] Hui-Po Wang et al., ProgFed: Effective, Communication, and Computation Efficient Federated Learning by Progressive Training, ICML, 2022.

[b] S. Reddi et al., Adaptive Federated Optimization, ICLR, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper present a new method for federated learning, focus on leveraging pretrained representation, which has its merits. The idea and the proposed methods sound novel, and I believe it is not hard to reproduce the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concerns are on the experiments. This work prepare their own federated learning setup using CIFAR-100 and PCam datasets. Actually, PCam is not popular in federated learning study. I believe following public bench and federated learning split can make this paper much better and more convincing. As a result, I vote this paper as "5: marginally below the acceptance threshold".

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed FedPEFT which is a set of several algorithms for reducing the model update payload size during fine-tuning large models with federated learning (FL). The algorithms include just fine-tuning the classification head, the biases and other techniques from prior works. The authors evaluated the methods on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 with various settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. The paper is straightforward and easy to follow.
2. The experiment setups are comprehensive including domain gaps, differential privacy and ablation study. 

Weaknesses

The main limitation is the novelty. The proposed methods are all based on existing parameter efficient approaches and simply applied in the FL setting. The technical contribution from this paper is very small.

Even though there are various experiment settings, the simulation on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 does not reflect the difficulties in heterogeneity issues in the real FL environment. Given this is an empirical paper, it’s hard to argue whether the proposed methods can be successfully applied in FL.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of writing is good while the novelty is very limited as mentioned above. The results should be easily reproducible since the pseudo-code and hyperparameters are given.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am leaning towards rejecting this paper given its limited novelty and contribution.

content.title: Exploring Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning for Improving Communication Efficiency in Federated Learning
content.abstract:
Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling the collaborative training of models without centralized access to the raw data on local devices. In the typical FL paradigm (e.g., FedAvg), model weights are sent to and from the server each round to participating clients. However, this can quickly put a massive communication burden on the system, especially if more capable models beyond very small MLPs are employed.
Recently, the use of pre-trained models has been shown effective in federated learning optimization and improving convergence. This opens the door for new research questions. Can we adjust the weight-sharing paradigm in federated learning, leveraging strong and readily-available pre-trained models, to significantly reduce the communication burden while simultaneously achieving excellent performance? To this end, we investigate the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning in federated learning. Specifically, we systemically evaluate the performance of several parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods across a variety of client stability, data distribution, and differential privacy settings. By only locally tuning and globally sharing a small portion of the model weights, significant reductions in the total communication overhead can be achieved while maintaining competitive performance in a wide range of federated learning scenarios, providing insight into a new paradigm for practical and effective federated systems.
